newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-U.S, Japan clash over photo-film markets.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-U.S, Japan clash over photo-film markets.

text.p: The United States and Japan on Thursday swapped charges of protectionism and misrepresentation as they took the first formal steps to put their photo-film dispute before the World Trade Organisation.

And while Japan blocked a U.S. request for early creation of a WTO panel to look into the row, Washington implicitly appealed to other trade powers to back a fight against what it argued was a range of Japanese barriers against foreign goods.

In a statement read to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB), Acting Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said the case revealed "discriminatory barriers" faced by outside firms on Japan's $9 billion-a-year market for photo film and paper.

But it should also concern other WTO members, the statement declared, because the barriers were "indicative of the exclusionary policies the Japanese government has implemented throughout the Japanese economy."

Her charges explicitly raised the dispute from one between the two world rival photo giants -- the U.S. Eastman Kodak and Japan's Fuji -- to the level of a potentially-damaging row between governments.

However, over almost certainly at least a year, the argument will be waged behind closed doors before a neutral three-man WTO panel -- creation of which will be automatically approved when the DSB next meets on October 16 -- and then an appeals panel.

The U.S. accusations were firmly rejected on Thursday by Japan's new WTO ambassador Nobutoshi Akao who dubbed them "totally contrary to fact" and insisted that the Japanese photo-film market was "fully open."
Earlier, Japanese officials and Fuji legal advisers -- including a leading U.S. trade lawyer -- had expressed confidence that they could convince a panel that there was no base for the U.S. charges.

Washington brought the case to the WTO after a long campaign by Kodak, which says it has lost $5,6 billion annually in potential sales since the mid-1970s because Fuji, helped by the Japanese authorities, has tied up the market.

But Japanese officials retort that Kodak failed in a sales drive in the late 1980s because its prices were too high and was slow to introduce new techniques into a market that naturally favoured the home producer.

They also point to the fact that while Kodak holds between only around 10 per cent of the Japanese market against 70 per cent at home, Fuji has only 12 per cent of the U.S. market against 67 per cent in Japan.

The United States has started a parallel WTO process under the 1994 world trade treaty accords on services, arguing that Japan's laws on the development of large-scale retail stores also discriminates against foreign photo goods.

It has also called on Japan for consultations outside the WTO procedures but based on a 1960 international accord on restrictive business practices it says are operated by Fuji to keep Kodak out of the market.
Akao told reporters he had responded to this request by seeking simultaneous consultations with the U.S. on restrictive business practices operating in the U.S. photo-film market.
Outside their home countries, Kodak holds 36 per cent of the global photo-film market and Fuji 33 per cent.
